claims.text: Corrosion resistance in steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily caused by formation of a protective surface oxide layer.
The proposed study concerns steel alloys with varying chromium and molybdenum contents.
The steels will be exposed to corrosive environments at different temperatures, pH levels, and chemical compositions.
Oxygen, moisture, and corrosive-substance levels will be controlled and varied.
Protective oxide-layer thickness and composition mediate corrosion resistance.
The protective oxide layer acts as a barrier to penetration by corrosive substances.
Barrier action by the protective oxide layer reduces the reaction rate between the steel and its environment.
Increasing chromium and molybdenum content produces a more stable and protective oxide layer.
Steels with higher chromium and molybdenum content will have greater corrosion resistance than plain carbon steel.
Plain carbon steel without alloying additions serves as the experimental baseline.
The hypothesis should hold over temperatures and corrosive environments typically encountered in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
The exact composition and structure of the protective oxide layer are not fully understood.
The role of alloying elements other than chromium and molybdenum is not fully understood.
The controlled study will measure corrosion rate, oxide-layer thickness and composition, and surface microstructure across steel compositions and exposure conditions.
Failure of higher-chromium and higher-molybdenum steels to show a significant reduction in corrosion rate would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe formation of the protective oxide layer would falsify the hypothesis.
